comparison.mainPoints: METHODOLOGIES BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Understand the need of agent-oriented methodologies • State different types of agent-oriented methodologies • Explain mobile agents by discussing the needs, issues and typology associated to it • Differentiate Telescript and TCL/TK 2 AGENT ORIENTED METHODOLOGIES • There is need for agent-oriented methodologies → centred around specific agent-oriented abstractions • The adoption of OO methodologies would produce mismatches - Classes, objects, client-servers: little to do with agents 3 AGENT ORIENTED METHODOLOGIES • Each methodology may introduce further abstractions - around which to model software and to organize the software process • For example: roles, organizations, responsibilities, belief, desire and intentions • Not directly translating into concrete entities of the software system → the concept of role is an aspect of an agent, not an agent 4 AGENT-BASED ANALYSIS • Analysis aims to understand, at least • What are the main actors interacting with the system • How the system interacts with these actors • What the system is supposed to do • Then, we associate accordingly • Roles responsibilities and capabilities • Interaction patterns between agents 5 AGENT-BASED DESIGN • Design aims to engineer, at least • What are the main components interacting within the system • What are the responsibilities and the capabilities of each component in the system • How the components interact to implement the system, i.e., the architecture of the system • Differently from analysis: we need to choose on which agents to use and how they interact 6 RELEVANT METHODOLOGIES • GAIA Methodologies • Encourages a developer to think of building agent-based systems as a process of organisational design • Agent UML • Extend Unified Modeling Language (UML) with agent features • Prometeus • Focuses mainly on the internal agent architecture → basically a methodology for designing BDI agent systems 7 MOBILE AGENTS 8 9 REMOTE PROCEDURE CALLS client computer server computer network client process server process MOBILE AGENTS client computer server computer network client process serverprocessagent vs MOBILE AGENTS Why mobile agents? • low-bandwidth networks • efficient use of network resources There are many issues when building software tools that can support mobile agents: • security for hosts and agents • heterogeneity of hosts • dynamic linking 10 MOBILE AGENT TYPOLOGY 11 We can divide mobile agents into at least three types Autonomous On-demand ‘Active mail’ AUTONOMOUS • By autonomous mobile, we mean agents that are able to decide for themselves where to go, when, and what to do when they get there (subject to certain resource constraints) • Such agents are generally programmed in a special language that provides a go instruction • best known example is TELESCRIPT 12 ON-DEMAND • The idea is that a host is only required to execute an agent when it explicitly demands the agent • Best known example → JAVA in html • A user with a JAVA-compatible browser can request html pages that contain applets – small programs implemented in the JAVA language • These applets are downloaded along with all other images, text, forms, etc., on the page, and, once downloaded, are executed on the user’s machine 13 ‘ACTIVE MAIL’ • The idea here is to ‘piggy-back’ agent programs onto mail • The best-known example of this work is the mime extension to email, allowing Safe-TCL scripts to be sent • When email is received, the ‘agent’ is unpacked, and the script executed → hence the email is no longer passive, but active 14 TELESCRIPT AND TCL/TK 15 TELESCRIPT • TELESCRIPT is a language-based environment for constructing mobile agent systems • There are two key concepts in TELESCRIPT technology: • Places → virtual locations occupied by agents.

[L12.1 - Result Sharing.pdf] WORKING TOGETHER 3: RESULT SHARING BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Explain result sharing through blackboard system and subscribe/notify pattern 2 RESULT SHARING • In results sharing, agents provide each other with information as they work towards a solution • It is generally accepted that results sharing improves problem solving by: • Cross-checking independent pieces of a solution • Combining local views to achieve a better overall view • Sharing results to improve the accuracy of results • Sharing results to allow the use of parallel resources on a problem 3 BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS 4 RESULTS SHARING IN BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS • The first scheme for cooperative problem solving → the blackboard system • Metaphor: A collection of intelligent agents gather around a blackboard, look at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: • All of the agents can see all of the blackboards (BB) all the time, and what they see represents the current state of solution • Multiple agents (KSs/KAs) can write solution on the blackboard at anytime without getting in any other's way 5 BLACKBOARD ARCHITECTURE • Main components: • A blackboard – a global database containing data and partial solutions / hypothesis • A set of Knowledge Sources (KS), or agents • A control mechanism 6 BLACKBOARD CONTROL MECHANISM • Blackboard systems must have some control mechanism: • Effective control requires to take into account: • Goal-directed factors: based on what an agent wants • Data-directed factors: based on what an agent is best able to do • Blackboard control is difficult because it can be difficult to determine the expected value of an action by an agent as there may be complex interrelationships among the agents 7 SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY 8 RESULT SHARING IN SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY PATTERN • Common design pattern in OO systems: subscribe/notify • An object subscribes to another object, saying “tell me when event e happens” • When event e happens, original object is notified • Information pro-actively shared between objects • Objects required to know about the interests of other objects → inform objects when relevant information arises 9 INCONSISTENCY • A group of agents may have inconsistencies in their: • Beliefs • Goals or intentions • Inconsistent beliefs arise because agents have different views of the world • May be due to sensor faults or noise or just because they can’t see everything • Inconsistent goals may arise because agents are built by different people with different objectives 10 HANDLING INCONSISTENCY 11 Do not allow it! For example, in the contract net the only view that matters is that of the manager agent Resolve inconsistency Build systems that degrade gracefully in the face of inconsistency Agents discuss the inconsistent information/goals until the inconsistency goes away SUMMARY • In today’s lecture, we talked about result sharing, focusing on blackboard system and subscribe/notify pattern • Next, we will discuss number of ways of having agents decide what to do, and make sure that their work is coordinated 12

comparison.mainPoints: PRACTICAL REASONING AGENTS: PRACTICAL REASONING AND INTENTIONS BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Describe practical reasoning • Relate practical reasoning with intentions 2 WHAT IS PRACTICAL REASONING? • Practical reasoning is reasoning directed towards actions — the process of figuring out what to do • Practical reasoning is a matter of weighing conflicting considerations for and against competing options, where the relevant considerations are provided by what the agent desires/values/cares about and what the agent believes (Bratman) • Distinguish practical reasoning from theoretical reasoning – directed towards belief 3 • Human practical reasoning consists of two activities: • The interplay between beliefs, desires and intentions defines how the model works COMPONENTS OF PRACTICAL REASONING 4 DELIBERATION • deciding what situation, we want to achieve • the outputs of deliberation are intentions MEANS-ENDS REASONING • deciding how to achieve these states of affairs • the outputs of means-ends reasoning are plans INTENTIONS IN PRACTICAL REASONING 1.

comparison.mainPoints: REACTIVE AND HYBRID ARCHITECTURES: HYBRID ARCHITECTURE BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Describe hybrid architecture • Layered approached • TouringMachine 2 HYBRID ARCHITECTURES • Idea: Neither completely deliberative nor completely reactive architectures are suitable → combine both perspectives in one hybrid architecture • Build an agent out of two (or more) subsystems: • a deliberative one: responsible for abstract planning and decision-making using symbolic representations • a reactive one: capable to respond to world changes without any complex reasoning and decision-making 3 HYBRID ARCHITECTURES • Meta-level control of interactions between these components becomes a key issue in hybrid architectures • Commonly used: layered approaches 4 LAYERED APPROACH - HORIZONTAL Horizontal layering: • All layers are connected to sensory input/action output • Each layer produces an action, different suggestions have to be reconciled 5 LAYERED APPROACH - VERTICAL Vertical layering: • Only one layer connected to sensors/effectors • Filtering approach (one-pass control): propagate intermediate decisions from one layer to another • Abstraction layer approach (two- pass control): different layers make decisions at different levels of abstraction 6 TOURINGMACHINES • Uses horizontal layering architecture • 3 sub-systems: • Perception • Control • Action 7 TOURINGMACHINES • Control sub-system consists of • Reactive layer: situation-action rules • Planning layer: construction of plans and action selection • Modelling layer: contains symbolic representations of mental states of other agents • The three layers communicate via explicit control rules 8 SUMMARY • Hybrid agents try to combine the speed of reactive agents with the power of deliberative agents • Uses layered approached – horizontal, vertical • We looked at TouringMachines as an example of application 9

comparison.name: L8.1 - Negotiation.pdf
comparison.mainPoints: REACHING AGREEMENTS 2: NEGOTIATION BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Describe protocol and strategies in negotiation 2 THE NEGOTIATION SET • The set of deals over which agents negotiate are those that are said to be: • Individual rational: agents won’t be interested in deals that give negative utility since they will prefer the conflict deal • Pareto optimal: agents can always transform a non-Pareto optimal deal into a Pareto optimal deal by making one agent happier and none of the others worse off 3 THE MONOTONIC CONCESSION PROTOCOL • Negotiation proceeds in rounds u where u ≥ 0 • On round u=1: • Agents simultaneously propose a deal from the negotiation set • Agreement is reached if one agent finds that the deal proposed by the other is at least as good or better than its proposal • If no agreement is reached, then negotiation proceeds to another round of simultaneous proposals 4 THE MONOTONIC CONCESSION PROTOCOL • In round u + 1: • No agent is allowed to make a proposal that is less preferred by the other agent than the deal it proposed at time u • If neither agent makes a concession in some round u > 0, then negotiation terminates, with the conflict deal • With this protocol, negotiation is guaranteed to end after a finite number of rounds • Either the agents will reach an agreement, or a round occurs where neither agent concedes. 5 THE ZEUTHEN STRATEGY Three problems: 1.

comparison.name: L10 - Working Together 1.pdf
comparison.mainPoints: WORKING TOGETHER 1 BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Understand the motivation behind Cooperative Distributed Problem Solving (CDPS) • Explain how CDPS can help agents to solve problems that are beyond their individual capabilities • Compare task sharing and result sharing • The contract net • Blackboard systems • Subscribe/notify pattern 2 WORKING TOGETHER • Since agents are autonomous, they have to make decisions at run-time, and be capable of dynamic coordination • Overall, they will need to be able to share: • Tasks • Information • No common goals if agents designed by different individuals • Important to make a distinction between: • benevolent agents and • self-interested agents 3 AGENT MOTIVATIONS Benevolent Agents • If we “own” the whole system, we can design agents to help each other whenever asked • In this case, we can assume agents are benevolent: our best interest is their best interest • Problem-solving in benevolent systems → Cooperative Distributed Problem Solving (CDPS) • Benevolence simplifies the system design task enormously 4 AGENT MOTIVATIONS 5 Self Interested Agents • If agents represent the interests of the general, then we cannot make the benevolence assumption • Agents will be assumed to act to further their own interests, possibly at the expense of others • Potential for conflict • May complicate the design task enormously • Strategic behaviour may be required COOPERATIVE DISTRIBUTED PROBLEM SOLVING (CDPS) • CDPS studies how a loosely coupled network of problem solvers can work together to solve problems that are beyond their individual capabilities • Problems faced by the nodes cannot be completed without cooperation • No single node has sufficient expertise, resources, and information to solve a problem, and comparison.name: L12.1 - Result Sharing.pdf
comparison.mainPoints: WORKING TOGETHER 3: RESULT SHARING BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Explain result sharing through blackboard system and subscribe/notify pattern 2 RESULT SHARING • In results sharing, agents provide each other with information as they work towards a solution • It is generally accepted that results sharing improves problem solving by: • Cross-checking independent pieces of a solution • Combining local views to achieve a better overall view • Sharing results to improve the accuracy of results • Sharing results to allow the use of parallel resources on a problem 3 BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS 4 RESULTS SHARING IN BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS • The first scheme for cooperative problem solving → the blackboard system • Metaphor: A collection of intelligent agents gather around a blackboard, look at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: • All of the agents can see all of the blackboards (BB) all the time, and what they see represents the current state of solution • Multiple agents (KSs/KAs) can write solution on the blackboard at anytime without getting in any other's way 5 BLACKBOARD ARCHITECTURE • Main components: • A blackboard – a global database containing data and partial solutions / hypothesis • A set of Knowledge Sources (KS), or agents • A control mechanism 6 BLACKBOARD CONTROL MECHANISM • Blackboard systems must have some control mechanism: • Effective control requires to take into account: • Goal-directed factors: based on what an agent wants • Data-directed factors: based on what an agent is best able to do • Blackboard control is difficult because it can be difficult to determine the expected value of an action by an agent as there may be complex interrelationships among the agents 7 SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY 8 RESULT SHARING IN SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY PATTERN • Common design pattern in OO systems: subscribe/notify • An object subscribes to another object, saying “tell me when event e happens” • When event e happens, original object is notified • Information pro-actively shared between objects • Objects required to know about the interests of other objects → inform objects when relevant information arises 9 INCONSISTENCY • A group of agents may have inconsistencies in their: • Beliefs • Goals or intentions • Inconsistent beliefs arise because agents have different views of the world • May be due to sensor faults or noise or just because they can’t see everything • Inconsistent goals may arise because agents are built by different people with different objectives 10 HANDLING INCONSISTENCY 11 Do not allow it! For example, in the contract net the only view that matters is that of the manager agent Resolve inconsistency Build systems that degrade gracefully in the face of inconsistency Agents discuss the inconsistent information/goals until the inconsistency goes away SUMMARY • In today’s lecture, we talked about result sharing, focusing on blackboard system and subscribe/notify pattern • Next, we will discuss number of ways of having agents decide what to do, and make sure that their work is coordinated 12

comparison.mainPoints: METHODOLOGIES BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Understand the need of agent-oriented methodologies • State different types of agent-oriented methodologies • Explain mobile agents by discussing the needs, issues and typology associated to it • Differentiate Telescript and TCL/TK 2 AGENT ORIENTED METHODOLOGIES • There is need for agent-oriented methodologies → centred around specific agent-oriented abstractions • The adoption of OO methodologies would produce mismatches - Classes, objects, client-servers: little to do with agents 3 AGENT ORIENTED METHODOLOGIES • Each methodology may introduce further abstractions - around which to model software and to organize the software process • For example: roles, organizations, responsibilities, belief, desire and intentions • Not directly translating into concrete entities of the software system → the concept of role is an aspect of an agent, not an agent 4 AGENT-BASED ANALYSIS • Analysis aims to understand, at least • What are the main actors interacting with the system • How the system interacts with these actors • What the system is supposed to do • Then, we associate accordingly • Roles responsibilities and capabilities • Interaction patterns between agents 5 AGENT-BASED DESIGN • Design aims to engineer, at least • What are the main components interacting within the system • What are the responsibilities and the capabilities of each component in the system • How the components interact to implement the system, i.e., the architecture of the system • Differently from analysis: we need to choose on which agents to use and how they interact 6 RELEVANT METHODOLOGIES • GAIA Methodologies • Encourages a developer to think of building agent-based systems as a process of organisational design • Agent UML • Extend Unified Modeling Language (UML) with agent features • Prometeus • Focuses mainly on the internal agent architecture → basically a methodology for designing BDI agent systems 7 MOBILE AGENTS 8 9 REMOTE PROCEDURE CALLS client computer server computer network client process server process MOBILE AGENTS client computer server computer network client process serverprocessagent vs MOBILE AGENTS Why mobile agents? • low-bandwidth networks • efficient use of network resources There are many issues when building software tools that can support mobile agents: • security for hosts and agents • heterogeneity of hosts • dynamic linking 10 MOBILE AGENT TYPOLOGY 11 We can divide mobile agents into at least three types Autonomous On-demand ‘Active mail’ AUTONOMOUS • By autonomous mobile, we mean agents that are able to decide for themselves where to go, when, and what to do when they get there (subject to certain resource constraints) • Such agents are generally programmed in a special language that provides a go instruction • best known example is TELESCRIPT 12 ON-DEMAND • The idea is that a host is only required to execute an agent when it explicitly demands the agent • Best known example → JAVA in html • A user with a JAVA-compatible browser can request html pages that contain applets – small programs implemented in the JAVA language • These applets are downloaded along with all other images, text, forms, etc., on the page, and, once downloaded, are executed on the user’s machine 13 ‘ACTIVE MAIL’ • The idea here is to ‘piggy-back’ agent programs onto mail • The best-known example of this work is the mime extension to email, allowing Safe-TCL scripts to be sent • When email is received, the ‘agent’ is unpacked, and the script executed → hence the email is no longer passive, but active 14 TELESCRIPT AND TCL/TK 15 TELESCRIPT • TELESCRIPT is a language-based environment for constructing mobile agent systems • There are two key concepts in TELESCRIPT technology: • Places → virtual locations occupied by agents.

BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS 4 RESULTS SHARING IN BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS • The first scheme for cooperative problem solving → the blackboard system • Metaphor: A collection of intelligent agents gather around a blackboard, look at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: • All of the agents can see all of the blackboards (BB) all the time, and what they see represents the current state of solution • Multiple agents (KSs/KAs) can write solution on the objects • Objects required to know about the interests of other objects → inform objects when relevant information arises 9 INCONSISTENCY • A group of agents may have inconsistencies in their: • comparison.name: L5.3 - Hybrid Architecture (1).pdf
comparison.mainPoints: REACTIVE AND HYBRID ARCHITECTURES: HYBRID ARCHITECTURE BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Describe hybrid architecture • Layered approached • TouringMachine 2 HYBRID ARCHITECTURES • Idea: Neither completely deliberative nor completely reactive architectures are suitable → combine both perspectives in one hybrid architecture • Build an agent out of two (or more) subsystems: • a deliberative one: responsible for abstract planning and decision-making using symbolic representations • a reactive one: capable to respond to world changes without any complex reasoning and decision-making 3 HYBRID ARCHITECTURES • Meta-level control of interactions between these components becomes a key issue in hybrid architectures • Commonly used: layered approaches 4 LAYERED APPROACH - HORIZONTAL Horizontal layering: • All layers are connected to sensory input/action output • Each layer produces an action, different suggestions have to be reconciled 5 LAYERED APPROACH - VERTICAL Vertical layering: • Only one layer connected to sensors/effectors • Filtering approach (one-pass control): propagate intermediate decisions from one layer to another • Abstraction layer approach (two- pass control): different layers make decisions at different levels of abstraction 6 TOURINGMACHINES • Uses horizontal layering architecture • 3 sub-systems: • Perception • Control • Action 7 TOURINGMACHINES • Control sub-system consists of • Reactive layer: situation-action rules • Planning layer: construction of plans and action selection • Modelling layer: contains symbolic representations of mental states of other agents • The three layers communicate via explicit control rules 8 SUMMARY • Hybrid agents try to combine the speed of reactive agents with the power of deliberative agents • Uses layered approached – horizontal, vertical • We looked at TouringMachines as an example of application 9

comparison.name: L8.1 - Negotiation.pdf
comparison.mainPoints: REACHING AGREEMENTS 2: NEGOTIATION BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Describe protocol and strategies in negotiation 2 THE NEGOTIATION SET • The set of deals over which agents negotiate are those that are said to be: • Individual rational: agents won’t be interested in deals that give negative utility since they will prefer the conflict deal • Pareto optimal: agents can always transform a non-Pareto optimal deal into a Pareto optimal deal by making one agent happier and none of the others worse off 3 THE MONOTONIC CONCESSION PROTOCOL • Negotiation proceeds in rounds u where u ≥ 0 • On round u=1: • Agents simultaneously propose a deal from the negotiation set • Agreement is reached if one agent finds that the deal proposed by the other is at least as good or better than its proposal • If no agreement is reached, then negotiation proceeds to another round of simultaneous proposals 4 THE MONOTONIC CONCESSION PROTOCOL • In round u + 1: • No agent is allowed to make a proposal that is less preferred by the other agent than the deal it proposed at time u • If neither agent makes a concession in some round u > 0, then negotiation terminates, with the conflict deal • With this protocol, negotiation is guaranteed to end after a finite number of rounds • Either the agents will reach an agreement, or a round occurs where neither agent concedes. 5 THE ZEUTHEN STRATEGY Three problems: 1.

comparison.mainPoints: WORKING TOGETHER 1 BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Understand the motivation behind Cooperative Distributed Problem Solving (CDPS) • Explain how CDPS can help agents to solve problems that are beyond their individual capabilities • Compare task sharing and result sharing • The contract net • Blackboard systems • Subscribe/notify pattern 2 WORKING TOGETHER • Since agents are autonomous, they have to make decisions at run-time, and be capable of dynamic coordination • Overall, they will need to be able to share: • Tasks • Information • No common goals if agents designed by different individuals • Important to make a distinction between: • benevolent agents and • self-interested agents 3 AGENT MOTIVATIONS Benevolent Agents • If we “own” the whole system, we can design agents to help each other whenever asked • In this case, we can assume agents are benevolent: our best interest is their best interest • Problem-solving in benevolent systems → Cooperative Distributed Problem Solving (CDPS) • Benevolence simplifies the system design task enormously 4 AGENT MOTIVATIONS 5 Self Interested Agents • If agents represent the interests of the general, then we cannot make the benevolence assumption • Agents will be assumed to act to further their own interests, possibly at the expense of others • Potential for conflict • May complicate the design task enormously • Strategic behaviour may be required COOPERATIVE DISTRIBUTED PROBLEM SOLVING (CDPS) • CDPS studies how a loosely coupled network of problem solvers can work together to solve problems that are beyond their individual capabilities • Problems faced by the nodes cannot be completed without cooperation • No single node has sufficient expertise, resources, and information to solve a problem, and different nodes might have expertise solving different parts of the problem 6 COHERENCE AND COORDINATION Coherence We can measure coherence in terms of solution quality, how efficiently resources are used, conceptual clarity and so on Coordination If the system is perfectly coordinated, agents will not get in each others’ way, in a physical or a metaphorical sense 7 COOPERATIVE DISTRIBUTED PROBLEM SOLVING (CDPS) CPDS addresses the following: 1. Problem decomposition: How can a problem be divided into smaller tasks for distribution amongst agents?

comparison.name: L12.1 - Result Sharing.pdf
comparison.mainPoints: WORKING TOGETHER 3: RESULT SHARING BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Explain result sharing through blackboard system and subscribe/notify pattern 2 RESULT SHARING • In results sharing, agents provide each other with information as they work towards a solution • It is generally accepted that results sharing improves problem solving by: • Cross-checking independent pieces of a solution • Combining local views to achieve a better overall view • Sharing results to improve the accuracy of results • Sharing results to allow the use of parallel resources on a problem 3 BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS 4 RESULTS SHARING IN BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS • The first scheme for cooperative problem solving → the blackboard system • Metaphor: A collection of intelligent agents gather around a blackboard, look at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: • All of the agents can see all of the blackboards (BB) all the time, and what they see represents the current state of solution • Multiple agents (KSs/KAs) can write solution on the blackboard at anytime without getting in any other's way 5 BLACKBOARD ARCHITECTURE • Main components: • A blackboard – a global database containing data and partial solutions / hypothesis • A set of Knowledge Sources (KS), or agents • A control mechanism 6 BLACKBOARD CONTROL MECHANISM • Blackboard systems must have some control mechanism: • Effective control requires to take into account: • Goal-directed factors: based on what an agent wants • Data-directed factors: based on what an agent is best able to do • Blackboard control is difficult because it can be difficult to determine the expected value of an action by an agent as there may be complex interrelationships among the agents 7 SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY 8 RESULT SHARING IN SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY PATTERN • Common design pattern in OO systems: subscribe/notify • An object subscribes to another object, saying “tell me when event e happens” • When event e happens, original object is notified • Information pro-actively shared between objects • Objects required to know about the interests of other objects → inform objects when relevant information arises 9 INCONSISTENCY • A group of agents may have inconsistencies in their: • Beliefs • Goals or intentions • Inconsistent beliefs arise because agents have different views of the world • May be due to sensor faults or noise or just because they can’t see everything • Inconsistent goals may arise because agents are built by different people with different objectives 10 HANDLING INCONSISTENCY 11 Do not allow it! comparison.name: L8.1 - Negotiation.pdf
comparison.mainPoints: REACHING AGREEMENTS 2: NEGOTIATION BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Describe protocol and strategies in negotiation 2 THE NEGOTIATION SET • The set of deals over which agents negotiate are those that are said to be: • Individual rational: agents won’t be interested in deals that give negative utility since they will prefer the conflict deal • Pareto optimal: agents can always transform a non-Pareto optimal deal into a Pareto optimal deal by making one agent happier and none of the others worse off 3 THE MONOTONIC CONCESSION PROTOCOL • Negotiation proceeds in rounds u where u ≥ 0 • On round u=1: • Agents simultaneously propose a deal from the negotiation set • Agreement is reached if one agent finds that the deal proposed by the other is at least as good or better than its proposal • If no agreement is reached, then negotiation proceeds to another round of simultaneous proposals 4 THE MONOTONIC CONCESSION PROTOCOL • In round u + 1: • No agent is allowed to make a proposal that is less preferred by the other agent than the deal it proposed at time u • If neither agent makes a concession in some round u > 0, then negotiation terminates, with the conflict deal • With this protocol, negotiation is guaranteed to end after a finite number of rounds • Either the agents will reach an agreement, or a round occurs where neither agent concedes. 5 THE ZEUTHEN STRATEGY Three problems: 1.

comparison.mainPoints: WORKING TOGETHER 1 BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Understand the motivation behind Cooperative Distributed Problem Solving (CDPS) • Explain how CDPS can help agents to solve problems that are beyond their individual capabilities • Compare task sharing and result sharing • The contract net • Blackboard systems • Subscribe/notify pattern 2 WORKING TOGETHER • Since agents are autonomous, they have to make decisions at run-time, and be capable of dynamic coordination • Overall, they will need to be able to share: • Tasks • Information • No common goals if agents designed by different individuals • Important to make a distinction between: • benevolent agents and • self-interested agents 3 AGENT MOTIVATIONS Benevolent Agents • If we “own” the whole system, we can design agents to help each other whenever asked • In this case, we can assume agents are benevolent: our best interest is their best interest • Problem-solving in benevolent systems → Cooperative Distributed Problem Solving (CDPS) • Benevolence simplifies the system design task enormously 4 AGENT MOTIVATIONS 5 Self Interested Agents • If agents represent the interests of the general, then we cannot make the benevolence assumption • Agents will be assumed to act to further their own interests, possibly at the expense of others • Potential for conflict • May complicate the design task enormously • Strategic behaviour may be required COOPERATIVE DISTRIBUTED PROBLEM SOLVING (CDPS) • CDPS studies how a loosely coupled network of problem solvers can work together to solve problems that are beyond their individual capabilities • Problems faced by the nodes cannot be completed without cooperation • No single node has sufficient expertise, resources, and information to solve a problem, and different nodes might have expertise solving different parts of the problem 6 COHERENCE AND COORDINATION Coherence We can measure coherence in terms of solution quality, how efficiently resources are used, conceptual clarity and so on Coordination If the system is perfectly coordinated, agents will not get in each others’ way, in a physical or a metaphorical sense 7 COOPERATIVE DISTRIBUTED PROBLEM SOLVING (CDPS) CPDS addresses the following: 1. Problem decomposition: How can a problem be divided into smaller tasks for distribution amongst agents?

comparison.name: L12.1 - Result Sharing.pdf
comparison.mainPoints: WORKING TOGETHER 3: RESULT SHARING BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Explain result sharing through blackboard system and subscribe/notify pattern 2 RESULT SHARING • In results sharing, agents provide each other with information as they work towards a solution • It is generally accepted that results sharing improves problem solving by: • Cross-checking independent pieces of a solution • Combining local views to achieve a better overall view • Sharing results to improve the accuracy of results • Sharing results to allow the use of parallel resources on a problem 3 BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS 4 RESULTS SHARING IN BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS • The first scheme for cooperative problem solving → the blackboard system • Metaphor: A collection of intelligent agents gather around a blackboard, look at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: • All of the agents can see all of the blackboards (BB) all the time, and what they see represents the current state of solution • Multiple agents (KSs/KAs) can write solution on the blackboard at anytime without getting in any other's way 5 BLACKBOARD ARCHITECTURE • Main components: • A blackboard – a global database containing data and partial solutions / hypothesis • A set of Knowledge Sources (KS), or agents • A control mechanism 6 BLACKBOARD CONTROL MECHANISM • Blackboard systems must have some control mechanism: • Effective control requires to take into account: • Goal-directed factors: based on what an agent wants • Data-directed factors: based on what an agent is best able to do • Blackboard control is difficult because it can be difficult to determine the expected value of an action by an agent as there may be complex interrelationships among the agents 7 SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY 8 RESULT SHARING IN SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY PATTERN • Common design pattern in OO systems: subscribe/notify • An object subscribes to another object, saying “tell me when event e happens” • When event e happens, original object is notified • Information pro-actively shared between objects • Objects required to know about the interests of other objects → inform objects when relevant information arises 9 INCONSISTENCY • A group of agents may have inconsistencies in their: • Beliefs • Goals or intentions • Inconsistent beliefs arise because agents have different views of the world • May be due to sensor faults or noise or just because they can’t see everything • Inconsistent goals may arise because agents are built by different people with different objectives 10 HANDLING INCONSISTENCY 11 Do not allow it! For example, in the contract net the only view that matters is that of the manager agent Resolve inconsistency Build systems that degrade gracefully in the face of inconsistency Agents discuss the inconsistent information/goals until the inconsistency goes away SUMMARY • In today’s lecture, we talked about result sharing, focusing on blackboard system and subscribe/notify pattern • Next, we will discuss number of ways of having agents decide what to do, and make sure that their work is coordinated 12

zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Explain result sharing through blackboard system and subscribe/notify pattern 2 RESULT SHARING • In results sharing, agents provide each other with information as they work towards a solution • It is generally accepted that results sharing improves problem solving by: • Cross-checking independent pieces of a solution • Combining local views to achieve a better overall view • Sharing results to improve the accuracy of results • Sharing results to allow the use of parallel resources on a problem 3 BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS 4 RESULTS SHARING IN BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS • The first scheme for cooperative problem solving → the blackboard system • Metaphor: A collection of intelligent agents gather around a blackboard, look at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: • All of the agents can see all of the blackboards (BB) all the time, and what they see represents the current state of solution • Multiple agents (KSs/KAs) can write solution on the blackboard at anytime without getting in any other's way 5 BLACKBOARD ARCHITECTURE • Main components: • A blackboard – a global database containing data and partial solutions / hypothesis • A set of Knowledge Sources (KS), or agents • A control mechanism 6 BLACKBOARD CONTROL MECHANISM • Blackboard systems must have some control mechanism: • Effective control requires to take into account: • Goal-directed factors: based on what an agent wants • Data-directed factors: based on what an agent is best able to do • Blackboard control is difficult because it can be difficult to determine the expected value of an action by an agent as there may be complex interrelationships among the agents 7 SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY 8 RESULT SHARING IN SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY PATTERN • Common design pattern in OO systems: subscribe/notify • An object subscribes to another object, saying “tell me when event e happens” • When event e happens, original object is notified • Information pro-actively shared between objects • Objects required to know about the interests of other objects → inform objects when relevant information arises 9 INCONSISTENCY • A group of agents may have inconsistencies in their: • Beliefs • Goals or intentions • Inconsistent beliefs arise because agents have different views of the world • May be due to sensor faults or noise or just because they can’t see everything • Inconsistent goals may arise because agents are built by different people with different objectives 10 HANDLING INCONSISTENCY 11 Do not allow it! For example, in the contract net the only view that matters is that of the manager agent Resolve inconsistency Build systems that degrade gracefully in the face of inconsistency Agents discuss the inconsistent information/goals until the inconsistency goes away SUMMARY • In today’s lecture, we talked about result sharing, focusing on blackboard system and subscribe/notify pattern • Next, we will discuss number of ways of having agents decide what to do, and make sure that their work is coordinated 12

comparison.mainPoints: WORKING TOGETHER 1 BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Understand the motivation behind Cooperative Distributed Problem Solving (CDPS) • Explain how CDPS can help agents to solve problems that are beyond their individual capabilities • Compare task sharing and result sharing • The contract net • Blackboard systems • Subscribe/notify pattern 2 WORKING TOGETHER • Since agents are autonomous, they have to make decisions at run-time, and be capable of dynamic coordination • Overall, they will need to be able to share: • Tasks • Information • No common goals if agents designed by different individuals • Important to make a distinction between: • benevolent agents and • self-interested agents 3 AGENT MOTIVATIONS Benevolent Agents • If we “own” the whole system, we can design agents to help each other whenever asked • In this case, we can assume agents are benevolent: our best interest is their best interest • Problem-solving in benevolent systems → Cooperative Distributed Problem Solving (CDPS) • Benevolence simplifies the system design task enormously 4 AGENT MOTIVATIONS 5 Self Interested Agents • If agents represent the interests of the general, then we cannot make the benevolence assumption • Agents will be assumed to act to further their own interests, possibly at the expense of others • Potential for conflict • May complicate the design task enormously • Strategic behaviour may be required COOPERATIVE DISTRIBUTED PROBLEM SOLVING (CDPS) • CDPS studies how a loosely coupled network of problem solvers can work together to solve problems that are beyond their individual capabilities • Problems faced by the nodes cannot be completed without cooperation • No single node has sufficient expertise, resources, and information to solve a problem, and different nodes might have expertise solving different parts of the problem 6 COHERENCE AND COORDINATION Coherence We can measure coherence in terms of solution quality, how efficiently resources are used, conceptual clarity and so on Coordination If the system is perfectly coordinated, agents will not get in each others’ way, in a physical or a metaphorical sense 7 COOPERATIVE DISTRIBUTED PROBLEM SOLVING (CDPS) CPDS addresses the following: 1. Problem decomposition: How can a problem be divided into smaller tasks for distribution amongst agents?

comparison.name: L12.1 - Result Sharing.pdf
comparison.mainPoints: WORKING TOGETHER 3: RESULT SHARING BAXI 3113 – INTELLIGENT AGENT Dr. Nur Zareen Zulkarnain Department of Intelligent Computing and Analytics (ICA) DG/1-18 zareen@utem.edu.my 1 LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Explain result sharing through blackboard system and subscribe/notify pattern 2 RESULT SHARING • In results sharing, agents provide each other with information as they work towards a solution • It is generally accepted that results sharing improves problem solving by: • Cross-checking independent pieces of a solution • Combining local views to achieve a better overall view • Sharing results to improve the accuracy of results • Sharing results to allow the use of parallel resources on a problem 3 BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS 4 RESULTS SHARING IN BLACKBOARD SYSTEMS • The first scheme for cooperative problem solving → the blackboard system • Metaphor: A collection of intelligent agents gather around a blackboard, look at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: at pieces of information written on it, think about them, and add their conclusions • Assumptions: • All of the agents can see all of the blackboards (BB) all the time, and what they see represents the current state of solution • Multiple agents (KSs/KAs) can write solution on the blackboard at anytime without getting in any other's way 5 BLACKBOARD ARCHITECTURE • Main components: • A blackboard – a global database containing data and partial solutions / hypothesis • A set of Knowledge Sources (KS), or agents • A control mechanism 6 BLACKBOARD CONTROL MECHANISM • Blackboard systems must have some control mechanism: • Effective control requires to take into account: • Goal-directed factors: based on what an agent wants • Data-directed factors: based on what an agent is best able to do • Blackboard control is difficult because it can be difficult to determine the expected value of an action by an agent as there may be complex interrelationships among the agents 7 SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY 8 RESULT SHARING IN SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY PATTERN • Common design pattern in OO systems: subscribe/notify • An object subscribes to another object, saying “tell me when event e happens” • When event e happens, original object is notified • Information pro-actively shared between objects • Objects required to know about the interests of other objects → inform objects when relevant information arises 9 INCONSISTENCY • A group of agents may have inconsistencies in their: • Beliefs • Goals or intentions • Inconsistent beliefs arise because agents have different views of the world • May be due to sensor faults or noise or just because they can’t see everything • Inconsistent goals may arise because agents are built by different people with different objectives 10 HANDLING INCONSISTENCY 11 Do not allow it! For example, in the contract net the only view that matters is that of the manager agent Resolve inconsistency Build systems that degrade gracefully in the face of inconsistency Agents discuss the inconsistent information/goals until the inconsistency goes away SUMMARY • In today’s lecture, we talked about result sharing, focusing on blackboard system and subscribe/notify pattern • Next, we will discuss number of ways of having agents decide what to do, and make sure that their work is coordinated 12

capabilities • Interaction patterns between agents 5 AGENT-BASED DESIGN • Design aims to engineer, at least • What are the main components interacting within the system • What are the responsibilities and the capabilities of each component in the system • How the components interact to implement the system, i.e., the architecture of the system • Differently from analysis: we need to choose on which agents to use and how they interact 6 RELEVANT METHODOLOGIES • GAIA Methodologies • Encourages a developer to think of building agent-based systems as a process of organisational design • Agent UML • Why mobile agents? • low-bandwidth networks • efficient use of network resources There are many issues when building software tools that can support mobile agents: • security for hosts and agents • heterogeneity of hosts • dynamic linking 10 MOBILE AGENT TYPOLOGY 11 We can divide mobile agents into at least three types Autonomous On-demand ‘Active mail’ AUTONOMOUS • By autonomous mobile, we mean agents that are able to decide for themselves where to go, when, and what to do when they get there (subject to certain resource constraints) • Such agents are generally programmed in a special language that provides a go instruction • best known example is TELESCRIPT 12 ON-DEMAND • The idea is that a host is only required to execute an agent when it explicitly demands the agent • Best known example → JAVA in html • A user with a JAVA-compatible browser can request html pages that contain applets – small programs implemented in the JAVA language • These applets are downloaded along with all other images, text, forms, etc., on the page, and, once downloaded, are executed on the user’s machine 13 ‘ACTIVE MAIL’ • The idea here is to ‘piggy-back’ agent programs onto mail • The best-known example of this work is the mime extension to email, allowing Safe-TCL scripts to be sent • When email is received, the ‘agent’ is unpacked, and the script executed → hence the email is no longer passive, but active 14 TELESCRIPT AND TCL/TK 15 TELESCRIPT • TELESCRIPT is a language-based environment for constructing mobile agent systems • There are two key concepts in TELESCRIPT technology: • ### 综合概述：智能代理方法论、智能代理及逻辑推理智能代理

在这三份文档中，我们讨论了智能代理的方法论及其在环境中的应用。《L13 - Methodologies.pdf》主要关注的是智能代理的方法论。它指出当前的面向对象（OO）方法学对于实现智能代理存在不足，因为传统的类、对象和客户端/服务架构并不能直接适应智能代理的需求。文档进一步阐述了不同的智能代理类型及其特点，并讨论了移动代理的相关问题与类型。

《L2.0 - Intelligent Agents (1).pdf》则强调了智能代理的本质以及它们在环境中的自主性行为，具体而言，它是通过一系列决策实现其目标的计算机系统。文档还介绍了简单的代理类型如恒温器（物理环境）。此外，《L3 - Deductive Reasoning Agents (1).pdf》进一步探讨了代理方法论、符号推理以及逻辑推理性智能代理的应用。

这三个文件之间存在一些重叠的观点，例如都强调智能代理在自主决策和实现任务上的能力。但也有明显的差异：文档一特别关注智能代理的方法论及不同类型的智能代理，而文档三则深入介绍了基于逻辑的推理技术及其如何用于开发智能代理。《L2.0 - Intelligent Agents (1).pdf》中的重点是识别代理行为与对象、人工智能系统之间的对比，并说明为何智能代理可以被视为一种有意图的系统。
